formula: event ~ factor(smkonset) + SexMale + cc + tv + (1 | class)
notes: Help example Surv.mixor <- mixor(Surv(smkonset, event) ~ SexMale + cc + tv, data = SmokeOnset, id = class, link = "cloglog", nAGQ = 20, IADD = 1), the "students in classrooms analysis" of grouped survival time (Hedeker, Siddiqui and Hu 2000). smkonset is the interval of smoking onset or right-censoring (1 post-intervention, 2 one-year, 3 two-year follow-up) and event whether the student smoked. RULE GAP: the table holds one record per student, not person-period records; the grouped-time survival model is rendered as the discrete-time hazard of the cigarette.dta ruling (HISTORY, Reading rulings: the indicator is the response, the period a categorical covariate) with the documented cloglog link, which leaves out the censoring of the grouped-time likelihood. student is a row id, int a column of ones and cctv the cc by tv product the model leaves out. The same TVSFP students are rabe_hesketh cigarette.dta. students.mixor (KG = 1) lets the SexMale effect vary across intervals on the same grouping, not a row. school, model 2's grouping, holds the classes and is ignored here.

formula: event ~ factor(smkonset) + SexMale + cc + tv + (1 | school)
notes: Help example School.mixor <- mixor(Surv(smkonset, event) ~ SexMale + cc + tv, data = SmokeOnset, id = school, link = "cloglog", nAGQ = 20, IADD = 1), the "students in schools analysis"; its grouping (28 schools) differs from model 1. smkonset is the interval of smoking onset or right-censoring (1 post-intervention, 2 one-year, 3 two-year follow-up) and event whether the student smoked. RULE GAP: the table holds one record per student, not person-period records; the grouped-time survival model is rendered as the discrete-time hazard of the cigarette.dta ruling (HISTORY, Reading rulings: the indicator is the response, the period a categorical covariate) with the documented cloglog link, which leaves out the censoring of the grouped-time likelihood. student is a row id, int a column of ones and cctv the cc by tv product the model leaves out. The same TVSFP students are rabe_hesketh cigarette.dta. class, model 1's grouping, is nested in school and ignored here.

formula: thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cc:tv + (1 | school)
notes: Help example Fitted.school <- mixor(thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cctv, data = SmokingPrevention, id = school, link = "logit") (Hedeker and Gibbons 1996, 2006): a random-intercept proportional-odds model of students in 28 schools. thksord holds the quartile (1-4) of the post-intervention tobacco and health knowledge score, thkspre the pre-intervention score; cc and tv are the randomized school arms, and cctv, their product, is written as the interaction cc:tv (as rabe_hesketh cigarette.dta). thksbin is the binary version of the response and int a column of ones. class (135 classes, nested in school) is model 2's grouping and ignored here.

formula: thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cc:tv + (1 | class)
notes: Help example, commented out as "students in classrooms analysis; not run": Fitted.students <- mixor(thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cctv, data = SmokingPrevention, id = class, link = "logit"); its grouping (135 classes) differs from model 1. thksord holds the quartile (1-4) of the post-intervention tobacco and health knowledge score, thkspre the pre-intervention score; cc and tv are the randomized school arms, and cctv, their product, is written as the interaction cc:tv (as rabe_hesketh cigarette.dta). thksbin is the binary version of the response and int a column of ones.

Help example Common.ICC <- mixor(TConcen ~ Mz, data = concen, id = ID, weights = freq, link = "probit", nAGQ = 10, random.effect.mean = FALSE) (Ramakrishnan et al. 1992): a probit random-intercept model of trouble concentrating in twin pairs with one intra-class correlation for MZ and DZ pairs. Each ID is one response pattern of a twin pair (two rows, 8 patterns) and freq counts the pairs with that pattern, standing on both members (as rabe_hesketh twin_hay): a frequency weight, ignored. Dz is 1 - Mz and int a column of ones. Varying.ICC (random effects on Mz and Dz, one variance per zygosity) keeps the grouping, not a row.

formula: Resp ~ Item1 + Item2 + Item3 + Item4 - 1 + (1 | ID)
notes: Help example Fitted.irt <- mixor(Resp ~ Item1 + Item2 + Item3 + Item4 - 1, data = irt.data, id = ID, weights = freq, which.random.slope = 1:4, link = "logit", nAGQ = 10, random.effect.mean = FALSE, UNID = 1), a two-parameter logistic IRT model of four ASVAB arithmetic reasoning items (Mislevy 1985). RULE GAP: the 2PL gives one subject effect an item-specific loading (random slopes on the four item indicators, unidimensional), which lme4 syntax cannot state; filed as its equal-loading (Rasch) form, a random intercept on ID. The four item indicators sum to one, as the source fits them without an intercept. Each ID is a response pattern by sex (32 patterns, four rows each) and freq its frequency weight (ignored, as twin_hay). Fitted.irt2 adds the SexItem1-4 products of sex and item on the same grouping, not a row; SexF stays a column.

Help example Fitted.norcag <- mixor(SexItems ~ Item2vs1 + Item3vs1, data = norcag, id = ID, weights = freq, link = "logit", nAGQ = 20): a random-intercept proportional-odds model of three four-category items on sex before or outside marriage (1989 General Social Survey; Agresti and Lang 1993). Item2vs1 and Item3vs1 code the item. Each ID is a response pattern (35, three rows each) and freq its frequency weight (ignored, as twin_hay). The non-proportional-odds (KG = 2) and scaling (KS = 2) variants keep the grouping, not rows.

Help example SCHIZO1.fit <- mixor(imps79o ~ TxDrug + SqrtWeek + TxSWeek, data = schizophrenia, id = id, link = "probit") (Hedeker and Gibbons 1996, 2006): a random-intercept ordinal probit of the four-category IMPS item 79 severity of the NIMH collaborative study. TxSWeek is TxDrug times SqrtWeek (the help calls it the TxDrug x Week interaction), written as the interaction, and Week is the raw time behind SqrtWeek. imps79 and imps79b are the 1-7 and binary versions of the response, int a column of ones. SCHIZO2 adds a random SqrtWeek slope and SCHIZO3 an independent slope with a logit link, on the same grouping, not rows.

aids.Rd fits no model; jointModel.Rd's example lmeFit <- lme(sqrt(CD4) ~ obstime * drug, random = ~ obstime | patient, data = aids) is the longitudinal submodel of a joint model with coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ drug, data = aids.id). survfitJM.Rd, anova.Rd, coef.Rd and residuals.Rd fit sqrt(CD4) ~ obstime + obstime:drug with a random intercept, and rocJM.Rd adds AZT, prevOI and gender, all on patient. CD4 already holds the square root of the count (JMbayes2's Baseline_Hazard article calls the same column the square root transformed CD4), so the source's sqrt is a second root. Time and death are the survival submodel's response, start, stop and event its counting-process form.

pbc2.Rd fits no model; jointModel.Rd fits fitLME <- lme(log(serBilir) ~ drug * year, random = ~ 1 | id, data = pbc2) with survreg(Surv(years, status2) ~ drug, data = pbc2.id), and ranef.Rd and plot.Rd repeat it. jointModel.Rd's second example takes random = ~ year | id and wald.strata.Rd, prederrJM.Rd and the competing-risks example take slopes or splines in year, all on id. years, status and status2 are the survival outcome. The other visit measurements (serChol, albumin, alkaline, SGOT, platelets, prothrombin, ascites, hepatomegaly, spiders, edema, histologic) stay columns, since no JM example models them.

prothro.Rd fits no model; xtable.Rd and simulate.Rd fit prothro$t0 <- as.numeric(prothro$time == 0); lmeFit <- lme(pro ~ treat * (time + t0), random = ~ time | id, data = prothro) with coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ treat, data = prothros), t0 marking the baseline measurement, written as I(time == 0); its interaction with treat stays in the formula only. pro is the integer prothrombin index (percent), a measurement, so continuous. Time and death are the survival outcome, start, stop and event its counting-process form. The same trial (Andersen et al. 1993) is joineR's liver.

aids.Rd fits no model and the help pages fit none to aids (variogram.Rd only plots it). The package's Baseline_Hazard article (vignettes/Baseline_Hazard.Rmd of drizopoulos/JMbayes2, the site DESCRIPTION names; not in the CRAN tarball) fits "a linear mixed model for sqrt(CD4) cell count", fm <- lme(CD4 ~ ns(obstime, 2) * drug, data = aids, random = list(patient = pdDiag(~ ns(obstime, 2)))), the longitudinal submodel of jm(coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ drug, data = aids.id), fm, time_var = "obstime"). pdDiag makes the intercept and the two spline terms independent; the spline names obstime once. CD4 holds the square-rooted count. Time and death are the survival outcome, start, stop and event its counting-process form.

README.md (the minimal example at the pin) fits a joint model of three longitudinal outcomes with coxph(Surv(years, status2) ~ sex, data = pbc2.id): fm1 <- lme(log(serBilir) ~ year * sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id), fm2 <- lme(prothrombin ~ year * sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id) and fm3 <- mixed_model(ascites ~ year + sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id, family = binomial()), filed as models 1 to 3; the JMbayes2 article fits the same with ~ year || id for ascites. jm.Rd also fits hepatomegaly by mixed_model(hepatomegaly ~ sex + age + year, random = ~ year | id, family = binomial()), a fourth response, ignored in every row. years, status and status2 are the survival outcome. The other visit measurements stay columns.

README.md (the minimal example at the pin) fits a joint model of three longitudinal outcomes with coxph(Surv(years, status2) ~ sex, data = pbc2.id): fm1 <- lme(log(serBilir) ~ year * sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id), fm2 <- lme(prothrombin ~ year * sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id) and fm3 <- mixed_model(ascites ~ year + sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id, family = binomial()), filed as models 1 to 3; the JMbayes2 article fits the same with ~ year || id for ascites. This row is fm2, the prothrombin time.

README.md (the minimal example at the pin) fits a joint model of three longitudinal outcomes with coxph(Surv(years, status2) ~ sex, data = pbc2.id): fm1 <- lme(log(serBilir) ~ year * sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id), fm2 <- lme(prothrombin ~ year * sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id) and fm3 <- mixed_model(ascites ~ year + sex, data = pbc2, random = ~ year | id, family = binomial()), filed as models 1 to 3; the JMbayes2 article fits the same with ~ year || id for ascites. This row is fm3, a mixed-effects logistic regression of ascites (No/Yes); the README at the pin correlates the intercept and slope.

prothro.Rd fits no model; the package's Posterior_Predictive_Checks article (vignettes/Posterior_Predictive_Checks.Rmd of drizopoulos/JMbayes2, not in the CRAN tarball) fits lmeFit1 <- lme(pro ~ time * treat, data = prothro, random = ~ time | id), "random intercepts and linear random slopes", with coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ treat, data = prothros) in jm(); lmeFit2 takes ns(time, 3) on the same grouping. pro is the integer prothrombin index (percent), a measurement, so continuous. Time and death are the survival outcome, start, stop and event its counting-process form.

formula: CD4 ~ obstime + obstime:drug + gender + prevOI + AZT + (obstime | id)
notes: aids.Rd and the joineR vignette describe the trial and fit nothing to aids. The page's source, Guo and Carlin (2004, The American Statistician 58:16-24), fits the CD4 trajectory separately (SAS PROC MIXED) and jointly with the time to death: time, time by drug, gender, previous opportunistic infection and the AZT stratum, with a random intercept and slope per patient; recalled from the paper's AIDS example, not read, so medium. CD4 holds the square-rooted count. RULE GAP: the source fits drug only through obstime:drug, but the row grammar needs drug among the covariates. time and death are the survival outcome.

joint.Rd's competing-risks example and the competing-risks vignette fit epileptic$interaction <- with(epileptic, time * (treat == "LTG")); joint(data, long.formula = dose ~ time + treat + interaction, surv.formula = Surv(with.time, with.status2) ~ treat, longsep = FALSE, survsep = FALSE, gpt = 3) with the default model = "intslope", a random intercept and slope in time per patient (Williamson et al. 2008). The coded interaction is the time:treat contrast of the two-level treat. The with.* columns are the withdrawal outcome. age, gender and learn.dis stay columns.

joint.Rd (and summary.joint.Rd, tidy.joint.Rd, glance.joint.Rd) fits joint(heart.valve.jd, long.formula = log.lvmi ~ 1 + time + hs, surv.formula = Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ hs, model = "intslope"), a random intercept and slope in time per patient num; jointSE.Rd the same with model = "int". log.lvmi is the column log(lvmi). grad, log.grad and ef are the other heart-function outcomes (grad is model 2), fuyrs and status the survival outcome. The other baseline covariates stay columns.

The joineR vignette (Model-fitting) fits joint(heart.grad.jd, grad ~ age + sex, Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ age + sex, model = "int") on the rows with grad observed, a random intercept per patient num. log.grad is the column log(grad); lvmi, log.lvmi and ef are the other heart-function outcomes (log.lvmi is model 1), fuyrs and status the survival outcome.

formula: prothrombin ~ treatment * time + I(time == 0) * treatment + (time | id)
notes: The joineR vignette (Model-fitting) fits joint(liver.jd, prothrombin ~ treatment * time + I(time == 0) * treatment, Surv(survival, cens) ~ treatment, max.it = 1000) with the default model = "intslope", a random intercept and slope in time per patient, "the sub-models ... used in Henderson et al. (2002)"; the sepassoc = TRUE variant keeps the longitudinal submodel. The baseline indicator I(time == 0) and its interaction stay in the formula only. prothrombin is the integer prothrombin index (percent), a measurement, so continuous. survival and cens are the survival outcome. The same trial is JM's prothro.

paquid.Rd fits no model; summaryplot.Rd fits paquid$normMMSE <- normMMSE(paquid$MMSE); paquid$age65 <- (paquid$age - 65)/10; m1 <- hlme(normMMSE ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + CEP, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", data = paquid), the one-class linear mixed model whose latent-class extensions (ng = 2, 3, mixture = ~ age65 + I(age65^2)) it and predictClass.Rd and predictRE.Rd fit. The vignette: "In the lcmm examples, MMSE is usually considered as the outcome", normalized by NormPsy's normMMSE. MMSE is an integer score 0-30, so count, fitted Gaussian on the normalized scale. Multivariate table: MMSE, BVRT and CESD, in the order mpjlcmm.Rd models them, are models 1 to 3; IST and HIER, the other repeated measures, are not modelled and ignored. dem and agedem are the dementia outcome; age_init, its entry time, stays a column.

mpjlcmm.Rd example 1 fits mult1 <- multlcmm(MMSE + BVRT ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + CEP + male, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", link = c("5-quant-splines", "4-quant-splines"), data = paquid), age65 = (age - 65)/10, then joins it with the dementia time in mpjlcmm(). RULE GAP: MMSE and BVRT measure one latent process, each through an estimated quantile-spline link, which has no registry family; family blank and the formula states BVRT's marker alone, so medium. BVRT is an integer score 0-15, so count.

mpjlcmm.Rd example 2 fits mCESD1 <- lcmm(CESD ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + male, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", link = "5-quant-splines", data = paquid), age65 = (age - 65)/10, a latent process mixed model then joined with MMSE and the dementia time in mpjlcmm(). RULE GAP: the estimated quantile-spline link has no registry family, so family is blank. CESD is an integer depression score 0-52, so count.

Help example fm <- lmer(Coloursaturation ~ TVset + Picture + (1|Assessor:TVset) + (1|Assessor), data = TVbo): 8 assessors score 12 TV sets (TVset by Picture), Repeat the replicate. The help lists 15 numeric response variables; multivariate table, so Coloursaturation, Colourbalance and Noise, in the page's order, are models 1 to 3, and Depth, Sharpness, Lightlevel, Contrast, Sharpnessofmovement, Flickeringstationary, Flickeringmovement, Distortion, Dimglasseffect, Cutting, Flossyedges and Elasticeffect are ignored. Repeat stays a column.
The help page lists Colourbalance among the 15 response variables and fits only Coloursaturation (model 1); that model on this response, the page's next in order, is proposed.
The help page lists Noise among the 15 response variables and fits only Coloursaturation (model 1); that model on this response, the page's next in order, is proposed.

Help example fm <- lmer(Preference ~ sens2 + Homesize + (1 + sens2 | Consumer), data = carrots): 103 consumers score 12 carrot products on a 1-7 scale, fitted Gaussian. sens1 and sens2 are product scores from a PCA of the sensory panel's averages; Product, crossed with Consumer, is not fitted and stays a column. Sweetness, Bitter and Crisp, the consumers' other 1-7 scores of the same products, are alternate responses.

Help example "Simple model for the ham data": fm <- lmer(Informed.liking ~ Product*Information + (1|Consumer), data = ham), 81 consumers rating 4 hams under 2 information levels (Naes et al. 2010), a 1-9 liking fitted Gaussian. The dontrun "big model" (Product*Information*Gender*Age with (1|Consumer) + (1|Consumer:Product) + (1|Consumer:Information)) is the start of step(), whose final model the page does not state, so not a row. Gender and Age stay columns.

epileptic.qol.Rd, the other help pages, the vignettes and the tests fit no model to this table. The page cites Jacoby et al. (2015, Epilepsia 56:460-472), whose abstract says the QoL data "were analyzed using longitudinal data models" and the continuous measures explored with joint models, with no specification I could read; the model is proposed: the score over time by arm with a patient intercept. Multivariate table: anxiety, depress and aep (the NEWQOL scores, higher worse), in the page's order, are models 1 to 3. The scores are integers (the help: continuous measures), so count, fitted Gaussian as linear joint models fit them. time is the day each questionnaire came back; with.time, with.status and with.status2 are the treatment-failure outcome.

mjoint.Rd's first example (and the vignette's comparison with joineR) fits mjoint(formLongFixed = log.lvmi ~ time + age, formLongRandom = ~ time | num, formSurv = Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ age, data = hvd, timeVar = "time"). Its second example, the README's and the vignette's, is bivariate: grad = log.grad ~ time + sex + hs with ~ 1 | num (model 2) and lvmi = log.lvmi ~ time + sex with ~ time | num, this row's response and grouping. hvd is the rows with both log.grad and log.lvmi observed. fuyrs and status are the survival outcome; grad, lvmi and ef the other heart-function measures.

mjoint.Rd's second example, the README and the vignette fit the bivariate mjoint(formLongFixed = list("grad" = log.grad ~ time + sex + hs, "lvmi" = log.lvmi ~ time + sex), formLongRandom = list("grad" = ~ 1 | num, "lvmi" = ~ time | num), formSurv = Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ age, data = list(hvd, hvd)); this row is its grad submodel. hvd is the rows with both log.grad and log.lvmi observed. fuyrs and status are the survival outcome; grad, lvmi and ef the other heart-function measures.

pbc2.Rd fits no model; mjoint.Rd's third example fits pbc2$log.b <- log(pbc2$serBilir); mjoint(formLongFixed = list("log.bil" = log.b ~ year), formLongRandom = list("log.bil" = ~ 1 | id), formSurv = Surv(years, status2) ~ age, data = pbc2, timeVar = "year"), and the joineR joint() equivalent with model = "int". The package paper (Hickey et al. 2018, BMC Med Res Methodol 18:50) fits a trivariate model of bilirubin, albumin and prothrombin time on the placebo arm, which the help page does not cite; not filed. years, status and status2 are the survival outcome; the other visit measurements stay columns.
